section_summary: This section consists of diplomatic records from the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo submitted to the Department of State between July and November 1936, including a schedule of July telegrams and comprehensive monthly political reports for August, September, and October (incomplete) 1936. The reports focus heavily on escalating Sino-Japanese friction triggered by violent anti-Japanese incidents in Chengtu, Pakhoi, Hankow, and Shanghai, accompanied by Japanese military and diplomatic pressures on the Nanking Government. They also detail Japanese domestic political maneuvers concerning administrative reorganization, electric power nationalization, massive military budget demands, right-wing agitation, and evolving relations with the United States, Great Britain, the Soviet Union, and Germany.

subfiles.about: Schedule of telegrams Nos. 144 through 164 dispatched by the American Embassy in Tokyo to the Department of State during July 1936.
subfiles.summary: This subfile comprises a one-page index schedule of telegrams Nos. 144 to 164 sent to the Department of State by the American Embassy in Tokyo during July 1936. The telegrams reported on major developments including the abolition of extraterritoriality in Manchuria, the death sentence and execution of Lieutenant Colonel Saburo Aizawa, and the sentencing of the February 26 insurgents. Other entries record queries regarding the proposed visit of the U.S.S. Alden to the Japanese Mandated Islands, commercial intelligence difficulties, the Automobile Manufacturing Industry Law, the repeal of martial law in Tokyo, and radio conference preparations.
subfiles.title: Telegrams Sent to the Department During July, 1936

subfiles.about: Covering despatch and monthly report on political, economic, diplomatic, and military conditions in Japan during August 1936.
subfiles.from: E. R. Dickover, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This subfile consists of the American Embassy's monthly report (Report No. 119) on conditions in Japan for August 1936, accompanied by an index and complete schedules of despatches and telegrams sent during the month. External affairs highlighted include ongoing negotiations with American oil companies under the Petroleum Industry Law, rising Sino-Japanese tension after the Chengtu mob violence and North China smuggling issues, diplomatic overtures toward Great Britain, the reception of the Brazilian Economic Mission, and Japan's strictly neutral stance on the Spanish Civil War. Internally, the report analyzes Cabinet debates over twelve national policies, contentious proposals for state control of the electric power supply, the Army's extensive budget demands and large-scale personnel rotations, gubernatorial changes in Korea and Formosa, and police preparations for the 1940 Tokyo Olympic Games.
subfiles.title: Despatch Transmitting Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of August, 1936 (Report No. 119)

subfiles.about: Covering despatch and monthly report on political, economic, diplomatic, and military developments in Japan during September 1936.
subfiles.from: E. R. Dickover, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This subfile contains the Embassy's monthly report (Report No. 120) for September 1936 along with its index and an annexed schedule of despatches sent during the month. Relations with the United States centered on Japan's announced retention of excess submarine tonnage under the London Naval Treaty framework and production restrictions imposed on Ford and General Motors under the Automobile Manufacturing Industry Law. The Sino-Japanese crisis deepened markedly after the Pakhoi murder of a Japanese subject and shootings in Hankow and Shanghai, prompting Japanese naval landings, demands for Chiang Kai-shek's direct negotiation, and warnings from Foreign Minister Arita. Domestically, the report details severe friction between Premier Hirota and War Minister Terauchi regarding administrative reform and electric power nationalization, comprehensive reshuffling of diplomatic chiefs of mission, planned tax increases, implementation of thought-control legislation, and the forced purge of labor unions from military arsenals.
subfiles.title: Despatch Transmitting Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of September, 1936 (Report No. 120)

subfiles.about: Covering despatch and the opening sections of the monthly report on conditions in Japan during October 1936.
subfiles.from: E. R. Dickover, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This subfile contains covering Despatch No. 2151 and the initial sections of Report No. 121 for October 1936, which is truncated at the end of page 205. The report records American-Japanese diplomatic exchanges regarding Sino-Japanese issues, Japan's refusal to permit the U.S.S. Gold Star to visit Palau, Truk, and Saipan, an agreement between foreign oil companies and Mitsui under the Petroleum Industry Law, and Japanese press reactions to Henry L. Stimson's book 'The Far Eastern Crisis'. It extensively analyzes high-level Sino-Japanese negotiations at Nanking between Ambassador Kawagoe and General Chiang Kai-shek amid stiffening Chinese resistance, as well as rising anti-British sentiment in Japan over alleged British financial and political backing of Nanking, Indian trade treaty abrogation, and police detention of British naval personnel in Keelung, Formosa.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2151 Transmitting Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of October, 1936 (Report No. 121)
